Period schedule:

Total: 4 periods · 2h 40min

section_titles: Where Are You Hiding? — Views of Objects
Boxy Buildings — Building and Drawing Multiple Views
periods.activity_title: Seeing the Same Object Three Ways

tasks_in_class.description: Look at the hide-and-seek picture; answer: (a) which game, (b) who looks from top, (c) if Rani faces hut in Scene 1 can she see who is hiding — discuss.
Mini, Bholu and Rani drew the same brick differently — discuss why; fill table: whose drawing shows top view, front view, side view.
Look at nine pictures of objects (TV, sofa, slipper, cup, school bus, chair, bolt, pizza cutter, helmet); write each object's name and which view is shown.
Collect empty matchboxes or boxes; build different buildings; draw their top, side, and front views; challenge friends to match drawing to building.

time_bands.activity: Open the hide-and-seek scene with the class. Students look at the picture together and work through Let Us Do Q1, p.24 ("Look at the hide-and-seek picture; answer: (a) which game…."), discussing what each character can or cannot see from their vantage point. The conversation surfaces the key idea that position determines what is visible.

Students examine the three brick drawings in Let Us Do Q2, p.25 ("Mini, Bholu and Rani drew the same brick differently…."). Working in pairs they discuss why the drawings differ, then fill the table naming which drawing is the top view, front view, and side view. Share responses across the class and agree on the vocabulary: top view, front view, side view.

Students work individually on Let Us Do Q3, p.26 ("Look at nine pictures of objects…."), writing the object name and view for each of the nine pictures. A quick pair-check follows where partners compare answers and reconcile any differences.

Each student collects two or three matchboxes and builds a small 'building', then draws its top, side, and front views on paper for the Boxy Buildings activity, p.27 ("Collect empty matchboxes or boxes; build different buildings…."). Partners swap drawings and try to identify each other's building from the three views alone.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often assume the front view is always the most informative; the brick task in Let Us Do Q2 is the right moment to challenge this — ask 'Could you tell the height of the brick just from the top view?' A common error is labelling the side view as the front view when the object is oriented at an angle; model holding the physical box while pointing to each face to anchor the vocabulary. The matchbox activity works best if students first build, then draw, so the physical object is always in hand as a reference.

section_titles: Where Are You Hiding? — Views of Objects
Cat Finds Jagat — Row and Column Positions
Grid Game — Describing Positions on a Grid
periods.activity_title: Matching Views, Then Mapping Positions on a Grid

tasks_in_class.description: Match the side/front/top view drawings made by Jagat and Rani with the correct 3D objects (pyramid, cube, prism/wedge).
Mark Jagat's position (3rd desk, 1st row); describe position of blue bag; identify object at middle desk of 2nd row; locate notebook; draw an apple at 3rd desk of 2nd row.
Fill Bholu's 3×3 grid using Rani's clues: eraser top right, pencil top left, apple at row 2 col 2, water bottle at row 3 col 2 (ball already placed at row 1 col 1).

time_bands.activity: Students open to Let Us Do Q4, p.27 ("Match the side/front/top view drawings made by Jagat and Rani…."). Working individually, they match each 2D view drawing to the correct 3D shape (pyramid, cube, prism/wedge). A brief class discussion follows: for each shape, students say which feature — flat top, pointed peak, rectangular face — helped them decide.

Introduce the cat-on-the-windowsill scene and the top-view classroom grid. Students work through Let Us Do Q1–5, p.28 ("Mark Jagat's position (3rd desk, 1st row)…."), recording row and column positions for each task. The teacher circulates and prompts: 'Which number tells us the row? Which tells us the desk?' to build precise use of the two-address system.

Students draw their own 3×3 grid and place objects using the verbal clues in the Grid Game activity, p.29 ("Fill Bholu's 3×3 grid using Rani's clues…."). After completing the grid, pairs check each other's placements by re-reading each clue aloud and confirming the row and column match.

periods.teacher_notes: The view-matching task in Let Us Do Q4 is a natural continuation of the vocabulary built around top, front, and side views — having students name the decisive visual feature for each match prevents guessing and deepens the concept. A frequent error in the classroom-grid questions is reversing row and column, calling the second desk in the first row 'row 2, column 1'; pause after the first question to establish a shared convention ('row = left to right across the room, column = front to back'). The grid game locks in the convention through immediate written practice.

section_titles: Drone Around the School — Aerial Top View
periods.activity_title: Navigating by Steps, Then Seeing from Above

tasks_in_class.description: Follow Mini's moves on the 4×4 grid (4 steps right; then 2 left, 1 up); mark Mini's final position; identify what object Jagat thought of.
Play the treasure hunt game with a partner on the 4×4 grid; give and follow step-direction clues to locate the chosen object.
From the starting point, trace paths to the flower and count steps for each path; determine whether mango or orange is reachable in fewer steps.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Drone Around the School activity, p.31
tasks_in_class.description: Circle the places or things visible in the drone top-view photograph of the school; write their names.

time_bands.activity: Students open to the Treasure Hunt example, p.30 ("Follow Mini's moves on the 4×4 grid…."). They trace Mini's path step by step — four right, two left, one up — marking the final cell. A class discussion asks: 'How is this different from just naming a row and column?' to surface the idea that sequential movement builds a path rather than giving a static address.

Pairs play the Treasure Hunt partner game, p.31 ("Play the treasure hunt game with a partner…."). One student secretly chooses an object on the grid and gives step-direction clues; the partner traces them and names the object. They swap roles at least once. The teacher listens for precise direction language (right/left/up/down) and prompts corrections as needed.

Students work through the Treasure Hunt path questions, p.31 ("From the starting point, trace paths to the flower…."), recording step counts for each path to the flower and comparing counts to decide whether the mango or the orange is reachable in fewer steps. A volunteer shares their reasoning aloud.

Students look at the drone top-view photograph in the Drone Around the School activity, p.31 ("Circle the places or things visible…."). They circle identifiable features and write their names. A brief share-out — 'What helped you recognise the playground from above?' — connects the drone image to the view vocabulary from the views-of-objects work.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error in the treasure hunt is confusing left/right direction after a turn — students who physically face the grid sometimes flip the directions; keep the class oriented to the same fixed direction (right always means east on the page). The path-counting task is the moment to introduce the observation that different paths between the same two points can have different lengths, which prepares the reasoning needed for the map section. The drone photograph works best if students first cover the labels and predict what they see, then uncover and confirm.
materials: Rulers or fingers for tracing grid paths

section_titles: Sight Map of School — Reading and Drawing Maps
periods.activity_title: Reading Routes, Writing Directions, Drawing Our Own Map

tasks_in_class.description: Trace the path from Grade 4 classroom to the stage on the school map; count how many routes you can find.
Identify which traced route is the shortest and explain how you know.
The water delivery man turned left from the entrance — write directions to help him reach the MDM Kitchen.
Draw a sight map showing the route from your school entrance to your classroom and any other important places.

homework.description: Rajat is unwell — choose the best route from the library to the medical room and describe it.
Trace Bholu's path (playground to IT room) and Rani's path (playground to sports room); compare which path is longer.

time_bands.activity: Students study the labelled school sight map and work on Sight Map Q1, p.32 ("Trace the path from Grade 4 classroom to the stage….") followed by Sight Map Q2, p.32 ("Identify which traced route is the shortest…."). They trace multiple routes using a pencil, count each, and then compare path lengths to decide which is shortest, writing a one-sentence explanation.

Students tackle Sight Map Q3, p.32 ("The water delivery man turned left from the entrance…."), writing step-by-step directional instructions for the delivery man to reach the MDM Kitchen. Pairs read their instructions aloud to each other and trace the described path to check it arrives at the correct room.

Students begin the Project Work, Let Us Do (Project Work), p.33 ("Draw a sight map showing the route from your school entrance…."). They sketch the key spaces they know — entrance, corridor, their classroom, any other rooms they can name — labelling each and marking a route with an arrow. The map is completed within this sitting; students share briefly with a neighbour at the end.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often write directions using cardinal terms (north, south) that are unfamiliar; encourage left, right, straight ahead, and then turn — language they used in the treasure hunt. A common error in Q3 and Q4 is omitting a turn at a junction, so model counting junctions on the map before writing. The project map does not need to be accurate to scale; the goal is that every labelled place has a route the student can describe in words.
materials: Crayons or coloured pencils (optional, for map labels)

items.section_title: Boxy Buildings — Building and Drawing Multiple Views
items.prompt: Riya stacked two boxes — a big one at the bottom and a smaller one on top. She looked down from directly above. Draw what Riya would see from the top view. Label your drawing 'top view'.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student's drawing should show two rectangles (or squares), one inside or overlapping the other, representing the two boxes as seen from directly above. The larger shape represents the bottom box and the smaller shape represents the top box. The label 'top view' must be present.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Look straight down at the object and draw only the outlines visible from that position.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student stack two actual boxes and look down from above before drawing; stretch: ask them to also draw the front view of the same stack.

exercise.description: Collect empty matchboxes or boxes; build different buildings; draw their top, side, and front views; challenge friends to match drawing to building.

items.section_title: Drone Around the School — Aerial Top View
items.prompt: A drone flies directly above a football ground and takes a photograph looking straight down. Which of the following would the drone's photograph most likely show?

options.label: A
options.text: A large rectangle or oval shape with markings inside it.

options.label: B
options.text: Tall goalposts with a net behind them.

options.label: C
options.text: Players running toward you with the ball in front.

options.label: D
options.text: The side fence of the ground with trees behind it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A — A large rectangle or oval shape with markings inside it. From directly above, the ground appears as a flat shape with boundary lines and field markings visible; vertical structures like goalposts and players are seen only from the side or front.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Imagine looking straight down: only flat outlines and markings on the ground are visible; tall vertical objects are not.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is picturing the front view of the ground, seeing vertical structures like goalposts, not a top view.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is imagining a ground-level perspective facing the players, not an overhead view.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is thinking of a side view of the boundary fence rather than looking down from above.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to look down at a book on the desk and describe what they see before answering; stretch: ask what the drone photograph of a swimming pool would look like from above.

exercise.book_ref: Drone Around the School activity, p.31
exercise.description: Circle the places or things visible in the drone top-view photograph of the school; write their names.

items.section_title: Sight Map of School — Reading and Drawing Maps
items.prompt: Think of the path you walk from the main gate of your school to your classroom every day. Draw a simple sight map showing that path. Mark at least two important places you pass on the way and label them.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student's map should show a connected path from the gate to the classroom, with at least two labelled landmarks (e.g. corridor, office, staircase, library). The map need not be to scale but the path must be continuous and the labels must match real or plausible school spaces.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw the space as seen from above, mark the route with an arrow, and label each place you pass.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student first describe the path in words and then convert each named place into a box on the map; stretch: ask the student to mark an alternative route to the same classroom.

exercise.description: Draw a sight map showing the route from your school entrance to your classroom and any other important places.

items.section_title: Where Are You Hiding? — Views of Objects
items.prompt: Priya, Karan and Meena each stand at a different position around a cylinder — one looks from the top, one from the front, and one from the side. Priya's drawing looks like a circle. Karan's drawing looks like a rectangle. Which view is Meena most likely seeing?

options.label: A
options.text: Top view, because the cylinder looks like a circle from above.

options.label: B
options.text: Side view, which also looks like a rectangle.

options.label: C
options.text: Bottom view, which looks like a triangle.

options.label: D
options.text: Front view, which looks like a circle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — Side view, which also looks like a rectangle. Priya's circle is the top view of the cylinder; Karan's rectangle is the front view. The remaining position is the side, which also yields a rectangle for a cylinder.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify which two views are already taken (top → circle, front → rectangle) and reason that the third position — the side — must be Meena's.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not tracked which view Priya already occupies (top → circle) and reassigns it to Meena.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student invented a 'bottom view' that gives a triangle, showing confusion about what a cylinder looks like from below.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confused the front and side labels, or did not track that the front view is already assigned to Karan.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student hold a cylinder (a bottle or tin) and look at it from each side in turn before answering; stretch: ask what all three views of a cube would look like and whether any two views are the same.

exercise.description: Mini, Bholu and Rani drew the same brick differently — discuss why; fill table: whose drawing shows top view, front view, side view.

items.section_title: Where Are You Hiding? — Views of Objects
items.prompt: Sohan looks at a sharpened pencil from the top (directly above the pointed end). He draws what he sees. What shape will his drawing be? Explain why.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: His drawing will be a circle (or a small dot surrounded by a slightly larger circle). Looking straight down at a pencil, you see the circular cross-section of the pencil body; the sharpened tip appears as a small dot at the centre. The length of the pencil is not visible from directly above.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Looking straight down at a pencil, only its circular cross-section is visible; the length disappears from this viewpoint.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to hold a pencil vertically and look down at it before answering; stretch: ask what the top view of the same pencil would look like if the pencil were lying flat on the desk.

exercise.description: Match the side/front/top view drawings made by Jagat and Rani with the correct 3D objects (pyramid, cube, prism/wedge).

items.section_title: Cat Finds Jagat — Row and Column Positions
items.prompt: In a classroom, desks are arranged in rows and columns. Ananya sits at the 2nd desk of the 3rd row. Rohan sits at the 3rd desk of the 2nd row. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Ananya and Rohan sit at the same desk.

options.label: B
options.text: Ananya is in a different row and a different column from Rohan.

options.label: C
options.text: Ananya is in the same row as Rohan but a different column.

options.label: D
options.text: Ananya is in the same column as Rohan but a different row.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — Ananya is in a different row and a different column from Rohan. Ananya: row 3, column 2. Rohan: row 2, column 3. The row numbers differ (3 ≠ 2) and the column numbers differ (2 ≠ 3), so both coordinates are different.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write out each student's (row, column) pair and compare the two numbers separately.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student did not read the two-coordinate address carefully and treated swapped numbers as the same position.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student compared only one coordinate (noting both have a '2') without checking which number is row and which is column.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student compared only one coordinate (noting both have a '3') without checking which number is row and which is column.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw a simple 3×3 grid, mark Ananya's desk and Rohan's desk separately, and then look; stretch: ask the student to name all desks that share Ananya's row or Rohan's column.

exercise.description: Mark Jagat's position (3rd desk, 1st row); describe position of blue bag; identify object at middle desk of 2nd row; locate notebook; draw an apple at 3rd desk of 2nd row.

items.prompt: Neel starts at the bottom-left corner of a 4×4 grid. He moves 3 steps to the right and then 2 steps up. Mark Neel's final position on the grid below and write its row and column number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Starting at column 1, row 1 (bottom-left): 3 steps right → column 4, row 1; 2 steps up → column 4, row 3. Neel's final position is row 3, column 4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Track horizontal movement first (right increases the column count) then vertical movement (up increases the row count from the bottom).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a printed 4×4 grid to trace with a finger before writing; stretch: ask the student to write a different set of moves that also ends at row 3, column 4.

exercise.description: Follow Mini's moves on the 4×4 grid (4 steps right; then 2 left, 1 up); mark Mini's final position; identify what object Jagat thought of.

items.prompt: On a grid, a star is 4 steps away from the starting point and a flag is 6 steps away from the same starting point. Sita says, 'It always takes more steps to reach the flag than the star.' Do you agree? Explain your thinking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, Sita is correct for any path that goes only right and up (or only in one direction at a time without doubling back). If the star is exactly 4 steps away and the flag is exactly 6 steps away from the same fixed starting point, then any path to the flag is longer than any path to the star — 6 is more than 4. The student should state that 6 steps is more than 4 steps and confirm agreement with Sita.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the step counts directly: 6 steps is always more than 4 steps from the same starting point.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw both paths on a small grid and count the squares along each; stretch: ask whether a path to the star could ever be longer than a path to the flag if you are allowed to go backwards.

exercise.description: From the starting point, trace paths to the flower and count steps for each path; determine whether mango or orange is reachable in fewer steps.

items.section_title: Sight Map of School — Reading and Drawing Maps
items.prompt: Look at the sight map of the school in your book. Priya says she can reach the stage from the Grade 4 classroom by two different routes. How can two routes both start and end at the same place but be different? Explain.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two routes can start and end at the same places but take different paths through different corridors, rooms, or open spaces in between. One route might go left at a junction while the other goes right and then turns back. The paths are different because they pass through different places even though the start and end are the same.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace each route on the map and notice that they go through different intermediate rooms or corridors before arriving at the same destination.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to trace both routes with a finger on the map in the book and name one place each route passes; stretch: ask which of the two routes they would choose for a hurrying person and why.

exercise.description: Trace the path from Grade 4 classroom to the stage on the school map; count how many routes you can find.

items.section_title: Sight Map of School — Reading and Drawing Maps
items.prompt: A postman enters the school gate and needs to reach the office. He turns right at the gate and walks straight. At the next junction he turns left and then walks straight again until he reaches the office. Write these directions as a numbered list so another person can follow them.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1. Enter through the school gate. 2. Turn right and walk straight. 3. At the next junction, turn left. 4. Walk straight until you reach the office. Any equivalent step-by-step list using left/right/straight language is acceptable.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert each movement (enter, turn, walk) into a numbered step using direction words: right, left, straight.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student first act out the moves physically in the classroom (turn right, walk, turn left, walk) before writing; stretch: ask the student to write the return directions from the office back to the gate.

exercise.description: The water delivery man turned left from the entrance — write directions to help him reach the MDM Kitchen.

items.section_title: Where Are You Hiding? — Views of Objects
items.prompt: A picture shows a round plate drawn as a circle. Which view of the plate does this drawing show?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — Top view. A circular plate seen from directly above shows its full round surface as a circle. The front and side views would show the thin edge of the plate as a narrow rectangle or line.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the shape seen and match it to the position: a full circle means you are looking straight down at the flat surface — that is the top view.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may think the front of a plate shows a circle, not realising the front view shows only the thin edge.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused side with top; both front and side views of a plate look like a thin line or narrow rectangle.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student introduced a 'back view' category not used in the chapter; the back view of a plate would resemble the front, not a circle.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to hold a plate horizontally and look down at it, then hold it vertically and look at it from the side, before answering; stretch: ask what the side view of the same plate would look like and draw it.

exercise.description: Look at nine pictures of objects (TV, sofa, slipper, cup, school bus, chair, bolt, pizza cutter, helmet); write each object's name and which view is shown.

items.section_title: Grid Game — Describing Positions on a Grid
items.prompt: Draw a 3×3 grid. Place a star at row 1, column 3. Place a heart at row 3, column 1. Place a circle at row 2, column 2. Which object is at the centre of the grid?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The circle is at the centre of the grid. Row 2, column 2 is the middle cell of a 3×3 grid, so the circle occupies the central position. The star is at the top-right corner and the heart is at the bottom-left corner.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Locate each object by counting to its row first, then its column, and identify that row 2, column 2 is the middle cell.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a pre-drawn 3×3 grid so the student only needs to place the objects; stretch: ask the student to add a fourth object at a position of their own choice and describe its row and column to a partner.

exercise.description: Fill Bholu's 3×3 grid using Rani's clues: eraser top right, pencil top left, apple at row 2 col 2, water bottle at row 3 col 2 (ball already placed at row 1 col 1).
